title: Majestic Fork
summary: Offer the rook between two opposing rooks, then use promotion checks and queen forks to recover material.

nodes.question: Can the rook fork two rooks without giving check?
nodes.explanation: After the illustrated bishop sacrifice and ...Rxf2, the black rooks stand on f2 and h2. Rg2 offers a rook that neither defender can safely capture without releasing a promotion.

branches.title: The h-rook accepts the offer
commentary: Begin after ...Rxf2 in the visually reconstructed seven-piece final phase. The earlier nine-piece setup and bishop interference remain source context.
Rg2 stands between the black rooks and attacks both. Capturing it abandons one promotion file.
Rhxg2 captures from h2, releasing the h-pawn’s promotion square.
h8=Q promotes because the h-file is no longer blocked by its rook.
Rxf7 removes the other pawn, but places the f-rook on the queen’s coming fork diagonal.
Qe8+ checks Kb5 along e8–b5 and attacks the rook on f7.
Kc5 is the illustrated escape from the check, leaving the rook attacked.
Qxf7 wins the forked rook. The resulting exact queen-versus-rook position remains a checked White win.
branches.explanation: Qxf7 wins the forked rook. The resulting exact queen-versus-rook position remains a checked White win.

branches.title: The f-rook accepts the offer
commentary: Compare the illustrated capture with the other black rook.
Rg2 creates the same double promotion dilemma.
Rfxg2 captures from f2, leaving f8 free for promotion.
f8=Q creates a queen while White still has a pawn on h7.
Ra2+ gives a rank check before Black collects the remaining pawn.
Kb8 answers the check while keeping the queen available for a checking fork.
Rxh7 collects the h-pawn but exposes the rook to the queen’s diagonal attack.
Qf5+ checks Kb5 along the fifth rank and attacks h7 along f5–g6–h7.
Kc6 escapes the check but cannot save the rook in this selected line.
Qxh7 wins the rook and leaves a tablebase-checked queen-versus-rook win.
branches.explanation: Qxh7 wins the rook and leaves a tablebase-checked queen-versus-rook win.

branches.title: Decline the capture and block the last pawn
commentary: The source also shows Black preserving the f-rook rather than capturing the offered white rook.
Rg2 offers the fork and forces Black to address the promotion threats.
Rxf7 captures f7 and leaves the h-rook available to capture.
Rxh2 removes that rook. White keeps one rook and the advanced h-pawn.
Rf8+ uses the surviving rook to check the white king.
Kb7 answers the check and starts the king’s approach.
Rh8 blocks the h-pawn directly, setting up the source’s last defensive attempt.
Kc7 walks closer while White’s rook protects h7 from below.
Kc5 follows the white king from two ranks away, seeking to hinder its approach.
Kd7 continues along the seventh rank toward the blockade.
Kd5 keeps the kings facing along the file in this selected route.
Ke7 advances along the same rank, keeping the pawn safe.
Ke5 maintains the distant opposition but cannot forbid the white king’s next step.
Kf7 approaches g7, where the rook on h8 will be attacked.
Kf5 follows but is too far to protect the blockading rook.
Kg7 attacks Rh8 and supports h8. White retains the exact win; the lesson stops before the source’s discontinuous final promotion display.
branches.explanation: Kg7 attacks Rh8 and supports h8. White retains the exact win; the lesson stops before the source’s discontinuous final promotion display.

exercises.prompt: Why does Rg2 work despite offering a rook?
exercises.answer: Each capture draws one black rook away from a promotion file. The new queen then checks while attacking the other rook.

exercises.prompt: What if Black preserves a rook to stop the last pawn?
exercises.answer: After ...Rf7 Rxh2 and ...Rh8, the white king can approach g7 with its pawn supported from below. The exact selected position remains winning.
